name: NetworkPolicy: default-deny + allow
objective: CKA › Services & Networking. NetworkPolicies are allowlists: once a pod is selected by any policy for a direction, everything not explicitly allowed is denied. Build a default-deny-ingress baseline, then open a precise hole (from a label, on a port). Graded on the policy spec (kindnet stores but does not enforce NetworkPolicy — the spec is what counts, same as the real exam's object checks).

questions.title: Default-deny all ingress
questions.teach:
A NetworkPolicy that selects pods and lists `policyTypes: [Ingress]` with **no ingress rules** denies all inbound traffic to those pods. Select every pod with an **empty** `podSelector: {}`.

**Gotcha:** pods are `default-allow` until *some* policy selects them for a direction — then they become default-deny for that direction. `policyTypes` controls which directions the policy governs; omit `ingress:` entirely to allow nothing in.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `default-deny` that applies to **all pods** and denies **all ingress**.

Target: `default-deny` has an empty `podSelector`, `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and no `ingress` rules.
questions.hint: `podSelector: {}` selects all pods; `policyTypes: [Ingress]`; and do NOT add any `ingress:` entries (that's what makes it deny-all-in).
questions.solution:
kubectl create namespace netpol-learn 2>/dev/null
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: netpol-learn }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
YAML

verification.description: default-deny selects all pods, policyTypes [Ingress], no ingress rules

questions.eli5:
Think of each pod as a house, and right now every house has its **front door wide open** — anyone can walk in. That's Kubernetes' default: until a rule says otherwise, all incoming traffic is allowed.

A **NetworkPolicy** is like hiring a bouncer for certain houses. The moment a bouncer is assigned to a house *for the "coming in" direction*, the rule flips: now **nobody gets in unless the bouncer has a specific "let them in" note**. No notes = nobody in.

A **default-deny** policy is a bouncer assigned to **every** house, with **zero** "let them in" notes. You do that by:

- **`podSelector: {}`** — an empty guest list that means *"this applies to every pod in the namespace."*
- **`policyTypes: [Ingress]`** — *"I'm only in charge of the 'coming in' direction."*
- **No `ingress:` section at all** — *"and I have no notes, so let no one in."*

That locks down all inbound traffic for the namespace. You then add precise "let them in" notes later (next step).

**Watch out for:**

- **Pods are default-ALLOW until some policy selects them.** The deny only kicks in once a policy targets them for that direction.
- **Empty `podSelector: {}` means ALL pods** — not "no pods." That's the opposite of what it looks like.
- **`policyTypes: [Ingress]` only governs inbound.** Egress (outbound) is untouched here; you'd need to list `Egress` to control it.
- **Deny-all-in = omit the `ingress:` key entirely.** Writing `ingress: []` means the same, but *adding* any rule under it would start allowing things.
- **This is namespace-scoped** — it locks down `netpol-learn`, not the whole cluster.
- On this bench **kindnet stores but doesn't enforce** the policy — grading checks the spec, exactly like the real exam's object checks.
questions.deepDive:
## Default-deny ingress — full rundown

### Mental model
NetworkPolicies are **allowlists**, evaluated **per direction, per pod**:
- A pod with **no** policy selecting it is **default-allow** for both directions.
- The instant **any** policy selects a pod for a direction (`Ingress` or `Egress`), that pod becomes **default-deny** for that direction — only traffic matching an explicit rule is permitted. Policies are **additive** (union of all that select the pod).

> "Deny all ingress" = select the pods for `Ingress` and give them **zero** ingress rules. The selection flips them to deny; the absence of rules leaves nothing allowed.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}          # empty = ALL pods in this namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress                # govern inbound only
  # no ingress: key  ->  nothing allowed in
```

### Reading the three key fields
| Field | Value here | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `podSelector` | `{}` (empty) | Selects **every** pod in the namespace. A non-empty selector would scope to matching pods. |
| `policyTypes` | `[Ingress]` | This policy controls **inbound** traffic. Omit `Egress`, so outbound is left default-allow. |
| `ingress` | *absent* | No allow rules → **all inbound denied** for selected pods. |

### Empty-selector cheat sheet (the classic confusion)
| Construct | Means |
|---|---|
| `podSelector: {}` | **all pods** in the namespace |
| `podSelector:` omitted at a `from` peer | n/a (peer must specify something) |
| `ingress:` key absent (with `policyTypes:[Ingress]`) | **deny all ingress** |
| `ingress: [{}]` (one empty rule) | **allow all ingress** (empty rule matches everything) |
| `namespaceSelector: {}` in a peer | all pods in **all** namespaces |

> Note the trap: **no `ingress:`** = deny all; **`ingress: [{}]`** = allow all. One empty rule is the opposite of no rules.

### policyTypes behavior
- `policyTypes: [Ingress]` → only inbound governed; egress untouched (default-allow).
- To default-deny **both** directions, select all pods with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and provide no `ingress:`/`egress:` rules.
- If you specify `egress:` rules, you **must** include `Egress` in `policyTypes` (and vice-versa) or they're ignored.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol
kubectl -n netpol-learn describe netpol default-deny
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol default-deny -o yaml
#   spec.podSelector == {}
#   spec.policyTypes == [Ingress]
#   no spec.ingress
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`podSelector: {}` = ALL pods**, not none. The single most common mistake.
- **Deny-all-in means NO `ingress:` key** (or `ingress: []`). Adding `ingress: [{}]` silently allows everything.
- **Policies are additive.** A later `allow-*` policy opens holes on top of this deny; you don't edit this one.
- **Direction is independent.** Default-deny ingress does **not** restrict egress — DNS and outbound still flow unless you add an egress deny.
- **Namespaced object.** It only affects `netpol-learn`; other namespaces are unaffected.
- **Enforcement needs a CNI that implements NetworkPolicy.** kindnet (this bench) and flannel do **not** enforce — the API object is still valid and is what's graded, mirroring the exam.
- **`apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1`** — not `extensions/v1beta1`.

### Quick reference
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: netpol-learn }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
```

questions.title: Allow from a label on a port
questions.teach:
On top of default-deny you open precise holes. An ingress rule with `from.podSelector` + `ports` allows only matching sources to specific ports. Multiple `from` peers in one rule are OR'ed; `podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` in the **same** peer entry are AND'ed.

**Gotcha:** NetworkPolicy ingress `from` selects **source pods**, while the policy's top-level `podSelector` selects the **destination** pods the rule protects. Mixing them up is the classic error.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `allow-client` that allows ingress to pods labeled `app=web` **only** from pods labeled `role=client`, on TCP port `80`.

Target: `allow-client` selects `app=web`, with an ingress rule whose `from` is `podSelector role=client` and `ports` is TCP/80.
questions.hint: Top-level `podSelector.matchLabels.app: web` (destination). One ingress rule: `from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: client}}}]`, `ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 80}]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-client, namespace: netpol-learn }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
YAML

verification.description: allow-client: dest app=web, from podSelector role=client, TCP/80

questions.eli5:
After the default-deny step, the houses labeled `app=web` are locked down — bouncer on the door, nobody in. Now you want to crack open **one specific door, for one specific type of visitor, through one specific entrance.**

A **NetworkPolicy allow rule** is exactly that note for the bouncer:

- **Which houses it protects** (the destination) — the policy's **top-level `podSelector`** → `app=web`.
- **Who's allowed in** (the source) — the rule's **`from`** → visitors wearing a `role=client` badge.
- **Which entrance** — the rule's **`ports`** → only TCP door number `80`.

So the note reads: *"For every `app=web` house, let in visitors badged `role=client`, and only through TCP port 80."* Everything else the default-deny still blocks.

The thing people flip around: **`from` picks the SOURCE (who's knocking), the top-level `podSelector` picks the DESTINATION (whose door).** They're different ends of the connection.

**Watch out for:**

- **`from` = source pods, top-level `podSelector` = destination pods.** Swapping these is *the* classic error.
- **Multiple `from` peers in one rule are OR'ed** — "any of these sources." List several and matching any one is enough.
- **`podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` in the SAME `from` entry are AND'ed** — "this label AND in that namespace." Put them in separate list entries to OR them instead.
- **A bare `podSelector` in `from` means "same namespace."** To allow another namespace you must add a `namespaceSelector`.
- **This is additive** — it opens a hole on top of default-deny; it doesn't replace it.
- **`port: 80` with `protocol: TCP`** — the port is the destination port on the `web` pods, not the client's port.
- On this bench **kindnet stores but doesn't enforce** — grading is on the policy spec, like the exam.
questions.deepDive:
## Allow-from-label on a port — full rundown

### Mental model
An ingress **rule** opens a precise hole in the default-deny baseline. A rule has two optional lists:
- **`from`** — the allowed **sources** (peers). Omit → any source.
- **`ports`** — the allowed **destination ports**. Omit → all ports.

The policy's **top-level `podSelector`** names the **destination** pods the rule protects. Don't confuse the two ends.

> Top-level `podSelector` = **whose door** (destination). `from` = **who may knock** (source). `ports` = **which door number**.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-client
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:                 # DESTINATION: pods this rule protects
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:                      # SOURCE peers (OR'ed within the list)
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels: { role: client }
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP            # TCP (default) | UDP | SCTP
      port: 80                 # destination port on the web pods
```

### AND vs OR — the peer rules
| Construct | Combination |
|---|---|
| Multiple **entries** under `from:` | **OR** (match any peer) |
| `podSelector` **+** `namespaceSelector` in the **same** entry | **AND** (label match **and** namespace match) |
| Multiple **rules** under `ingress:` | **OR** (allowed if any rule matches) |
| `from` **and** `ports` in one rule | **AND** (must satisfy both) |

```yaml
# OR: client pods, OR anything in monitoring namespace
from:
- podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }
- namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: monitoring } }

# AND: pods labeled role=client that are ALSO in the monitoring namespace
from:
- podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }
  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: monitoring } }
```

### Peer types in `from`
| Peer | Selects |
|---|---|
| `podSelector` | Pods **in the policy's namespace** matching labels. |
| `namespaceSelector` | All pods in **matching namespaces**. |
| `podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` | Matching pods **within** matching namespaces (AND). |
| `ipBlock` | CIDR range (with optional `except:`); for external/IP sources. |

> A lone `podSelector` in `from` is **same-namespace only**. Add a `namespaceSelector` to reach across namespaces.

### Ports
```yaml
ports:
- protocol: TCP
  port: 80            # numeric or a named containerPort
# - port: 8000        # endPort: 9000   # port RANGE (needs cluster support)
```
- `port` is the **destination** port on the selected (destination) pods.
- May be a **named** port referencing the container's `ports[].name`.
- `endPort` defines a range `[port, endPort]` (feature-gated/CNI-dependent).

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn describe netpol allow-client
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-client -o yaml
#   spec.podSelector.matchLabels.app == web          (destination)
#   spec.ingress[0].from[0].podSelector role=client  (source)
#   spec.ingress[0].ports[0] == {TCP, 80}
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`from` = source, top-level `podSelector` = destination.** The #1 mistake — graders check both ends.
- **OR vs AND hinges on list structure:** separate `-` entries OR; two selectors under one entry AND. A stray dash changes the meaning.
- **Bare `podSelector` in `from` is same-namespace.** Cross-namespace needs `namespaceSelector`.
- **Policies are additive**, not override — this rule opens a hole over the default-deny; deleting default-deny doesn't require touching this.
- **Omitting `ports`** allows **all** ports from the matched sources; omitting `from` allows the ports from **any** source.
- **`ingress: [{}]`** (empty rule) = allow all — very different from a scoped rule.
- Enforcement needs a policy-aware CNI; kindnet/flannel store but don't enforce. The **spec is graded**, as on the exam.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }     # destination
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }   # source
    ports:
    - { protocol: TCP, port: 80 }
```
